headline: Bunker Boils Off the Lighthouse While Montauk's Albie Water Finally Stacks Up
subhead: Fluke are paying the bills on the reefs, blues are shredding bait on the surface, and the temperature line every fall-run angler watches just crossed into trigger range.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

There's a specific week in every Montauk season where the Point stops being about grinding out summer fluke and starts holding its breath for what comes next. This is that week. Water off the Lighthouse is sitting around 74.5 degrees, and anybody who's fished this rock long enough knows what that number means — it's the trigger water. Not blitz water yet. Trigger water. The stuff that turns a quiet ocean into false albacore and bonito territory almost overnight. We flagged this exact shift last week, that surface temps were nosing into the high 60s and low 70s and the first confirmed albie catches would follow close behind. We haven't gotten that confirmation yet — nobody's iron off the Point this week that I'd call verified — but the water's sitting right where it needs to be, and that's not nothing.

While we wait on the speedsters, the bunker pods have been doing the talking. Big, dense schools have been holding off the south side and around Shagwong, and where they concentrate, the blues have been merciless. Topwater blowups on bunker schools have been a daily event whenever the wind lays down enough to see them working — poppers and big Danny-style swimmers thrown right into the foam have been drawing violent strikes, the kind of surface explosion that reminds you why bluefish get overlooked around here even though they shouldn't be. This pattern holds as long as the bunker stay thick and the high pressure keeps the ocean side fishable, and right now both of those boxes are checked. Buoy readings out in the Bight are showing 3.6-foot swell on a short six-second period — not glass, but workable, and it hasn't been enough to shut the bunker pods down or push them off the structure.

Fluke have been the steadiest producers of the week, and that's typical for early August — the mercury climbs, the bass get lazy in the heat, and the flatties take center stage on the reefs. Drifts across Shagwong Reef and the deeper water off North Bar in 30 to 45 feet have been holding fish, with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails outproducing bare bucktails on the slower outgoing tide. When the current's really moving — the back half of the ebb out there is no joke — a heavier one-ounce head keeps you in contact with bottom instead of getting swept up into the water column. Keeper-class fish have been mixed with plenty of shorts, so it's been a numbers game more than a sure thing, but there've been fish to four and five pounds coming out of that stretch for anglers willing to make multiple drifts and stay on the same piece of structure.

Striped bass have been the tougher assignment, and I won't pretend otherwise. Daytime summer bass fishing at the Point is a grind — the boulder field off the Lighthouse still holds fish, but in this heat they've pulled deeper into the current seams and they're feeding hardest in that narrow window around first light and again after dark. Eels fished slow along the rock structure on the building tide, right where the white water meets the boulders, have been the most consistent producer for anybody working the surf at night. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig off the same stretch have picked up a few too, though the bite's been more opportunistic than predictable. If you're set up to fish through the night, the two hours around the tide change — either side — have been the windows worth having a rod in your hand.

Porgies are doing what porgies do this time of year, which is to say they're reliable and unglamorous and exactly what you want when the bigger stuff is being difficult. Clams and sandworms fished on high-low rigs over the Shagwong bottom and around Frisbee Bank have kept rods bent for anybody who wants steady action without much drama. Turtle Cove has been holding some smaller fish close to shore as well, worth a look if you're fishing light tackle from the rocks and want something to do between bass shifts.

Fort Pond Bay and the harbor side have been quieter this stretch, which tracks with the calendar — that shoreline really turns on with the fall push of bait into the bay come September, and we're not there yet. Lake Montauk's west side has still been worth a drift for fluke on the outgoing, especially near the inlet where the current concentrates bait against the bulkheads, but nothing to suggest it's outfishing the ocean-side reefs right now.

Looking ahead, the whole story this week is that temperature line. If it holds or creeps higher through the next several days without a hard cold-water upwelling event, I'd expect the first legitimate albie and bonito sightings to show around the rips east of the Point and along the north side structure — that's historically where they show first once the water's ready. I wouldn't restructure a whole trip around it yet, but I'd have a bag of small metal and epoxy jigs rigged and ready in the truck. In the meantime, the bunker-blitz pattern on the blues is the most dependable thing happening on this beat, and the fluke bite on the reefs is worth the boat ride if numbers matter more to you than size. Bass anglers, I'd focus effort on the dark hours and treat daytime bites as a bonus, not a plan.
